content:
If arthritis and frailty mean you need help at home, your council may offer care services after an assessment. Direct Payments are another way to receive that support.

This guide explains the basics. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

What are Direct Payments?

Payments from your council to arrange your own care. They are available in all UK nations, though rules differ.

Who can get them

  • People assessed as having eligible care needs.
  • Carers who have eligible support needs.
  • Someone can manage them on your behalf.

What they can pay for

  • Care workers or personal assistants.
  • Agency care.
  • Some equipment or activities that meet your assessed needs.

Things to consider

  • You must keep records and show how money was spent.
  • Employing a personal assistant brings employer responsibilities.
  • Support services can help with payroll and paperwork.

How to apply

Ask your council for a needs assessment, then ask about Direct Payments.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Do Direct Payments affect benefits?

They are not counted as income for benefits. Check with an advice service.

Can I pay a family member?

Usually not a close relative living with you, except in some circumstances. Ask your council.

Sources and further reading

  • GOV.UK: Apply for a needs assessment by social services
